issues.legal_issue: An unlawful assembly may be found despite the acquittal of most accused when the evidence supports that more than five persons took part and the participants were not definitively limited to the named accused.
material_facts: Thirteen persons were charged, but only three were found to have participated and convicted; the others were acquitted because their participation was not proved beyond doubt.
The trial court considered that the three convicted persons were accompanied by nine or ten others, though it could not identify them.
Some prosecution witnesses named fewer than all thirteen accused, while witnesses stated that thirteen persons were in the appellant’s party.
issues.conclusion: The courts below could find that more than five persons formed the appellant’s party, so the acquittals did not prevent a finding that the party was an unlawful assembly.
issues.legal_principle: Under sections 141 and 149 of the Indian Penal Code, an assembly of five or more persons may be an unlawful assembly and its members may incur constructive liability. Where the alleged assailants are a definite group and all are named, acquittal of enough named persons to leave fewer than five means the assembly requirement is not met; that limitation did not apply on this evidence. The Court referred to Dalip Singh v. State of Punjab, [1954] S.C.R. 145.

predicates.criminal_appeal_against_group_liability_: The proceeding is an appeal against a conviction based on the accused’s participation in a group.
predicates.evidence_supports_more_than_five_partici: The evidence supports that more than five persons took part on the accused’s side.
predicates.participants_not_definitively_limited_to: The evidence does not establish that the participating group was definitively limited to a fully identified set of named accused.

issues.definition: When an appeal concerns group liability, the evidence supports more than five participants, and the participants are not definitively limited to named accused, acquittals do not by themselves prevent an unlawful-assembly finding.

issues.legal_issue: A participant in a preconcerted, armed free fight cannot rely on private defence, and may be constructively liable for offences committed by others in furtherance of the group’s common object.
material_facts: Both parties gathered persons armed with deadly weapons for a preconcerted fight over a land dispute.
The appellant participated in the fight and was armed; members of the opposing party suffered injuries, and one died.
The appellant was not proved to have personally inflicted an injury on the deceased.
issues.conclusion: The appellant’s party had a common object to fight and cause injuries, and the appellant could be held constructively liable under section 149 for the offences committed in furtherance of that object.
issues.legal_principle: Under sections 149, 302 and 307 of the Indian Penal Code, a member of an unlawful assembly is liable for offences committed in prosecution of its common object or those the members knew were likely to be committed. A party that prepares and arms itself for a preconcerted free fight has no right of private defence; its intention to fight and cause injuries can constitute a common object. The Court relied on Gore Lal v. State of U.P., Criminal Appeal No. 129 of 1959, decided December 15, 1960.

predicates.criminal_appeal_against_group_offence_co: The proceeding is an appeal against a conviction for an offence attributed to a group.
predicates.accused_participated_in_preconcerted_arm: The accused joined a fight that the parties had prepared for in advance and the accused’s side went armed.
predicates.group_intended_to_cause_injuries: The accused’s group intended to fight and cause injuries to the opposing party.
predicates.no_right_of_private_defence: The circumstances show that the accused’s side had no right to defend itself against the opposing party.

issues.definition: A participant in an armed fight prepared for in advance, where the group intended to injure its opponents and had no right of private defence, may be held liable for group offences even without personally inflicting the injury.

issues.legal_issue: Where the evidence does not establish an unlawful assembly of five or more, a conviction may still be sustained under section 34 if the accused shared a common intention to attack and cause injuries capable of resulting in death.
material_facts: The appellant and the other convicted persons went armed and determined to fight the opposing party.
The facts supported a common intention to attack and cause injuries that might result in death.
The appellant was not proved to have personally caused an injury to the deceased, and his lack of involvement in the land dispute did not prevent him from sharing that intention.
issues.conclusion: Even if the finding that more than five persons were in the appellant’s party was wrong, the convictions under sections 302 and 307 could be converted to convictions under those sections read with section 34.
issues.legal_principle: Section 34 of the Indian Penal Code imposes joint liability for a criminal act done by several persons in furtherance of their common intention. The Court considered the accused’s armed and determined participation and the intended attack, and held that personal infliction of an injury was not necessary to sustain liability on that basis.

predicates.criminal_appeal_against_group_offence_co: The proceeding is an appeal against a conviction for an offence attributed to joint action.
predicates.accused_went_armed_and_determined_to_fig: The accused went with companions while armed and determined to engage in a fight.
predicates.shared_intention_to_attack_and_cause_pot: The accused shared the intention to attack the opposing party and cause injuries capable of resulting in death.

issues.definition: When an accused appeals a group-offence conviction and went armed and determined to fight while sharing an intention to cause potentially fatal injuries, the conviction may rest on common intention even if the accused did not personally inflict the injury.
